hook_text: Some of the most crowded land on earth didn't exist until a river carried it there, one grain of mud at a time.
clip_script: A river carries mud. Lots of it. When it floods, water spills over its banks and slows down, and drops its heavy sand right beside the river. Flood after flood, the sand builds raised banks called levees. When the river reaches a calm sea, it slows right down and drops everything. The mud piles up until it rises out of the water. New land. A delta. The river splits into fingers that spread out like a fan. Egypt's Nile Delta has fed people for thousands of years. Bangladesh sits on the biggest delta on earth. And Botswana's Okavango is a delta that never reaches the sea at all. But this land is low and flat. When levees break, as in New Orleans in 2005, the water pours in.
visual_style: Muddy floodwater spilling over a riverbank; sand ridges growing along a river; a satellite view of the Nile Delta's green fan; a river splitting into channels; the Okavango's lagoons with elephants; a flooded city street.
pacing: Steady build of land, then a sudden break at the flood.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn how levees and deltas form and why people live on them.
